body.p: The undersigned thanks the Examiner for the courtesy of a video interview conducted on August 26, 2021 with the undersigned and with Qimin Quan, one of the inventors on the instant application. The present response addresses substantive points discussed during the interview, as discussed below. Accordingly, the present response is believed to constitute a complete written statement of the reasons presented at the interview as warranting favorable action, as required by 37 C.F.R. § 1.133(b).
Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 43, 47 and 135-146 were previously pending in this application.

By this amendment, claim 1 has been amended and is supported by the specification as originally filed, for example, on pg. 5, lines 25-33; pg. 6, lines 12-14; pg. 6, lines 22-24; pg. 10, lines 26-33; pg. 11, lines 11-13; pg. 13, lines 17-21; pg. 18, lines 13-20; pg. 18, line 31 to pg. 19, line 9, and FIGs. iF and 1G. Claims 43 and 146 have been cancelled without prejudice or disclaimer.
No new matter has been added. Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 47, and 135-145 are currently pending in this application for examination, with claim 1 being independent.

h1.u: 103 in view of Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa

body.p: Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 43, 47, and 135-141 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Rylander, et al., U.S. Pat. Apl. Pub. No. 2013/0338627 ("Rylander") in view of Szunerits, et al., "Sensing using Localised Surface Plasmon Resonance Sensors," Chem. Comm., 2012, 48, 8999-9010 ("Szunerits"), and further in view of Hosokawa, et al., Nanoparticle Technology Handbook, 2007, pg. 365 ("Hosokawa"). The Office Action alleges that Rylander generally teaches claim 1, except that Rylander does not teach at least one particle attached to the end portion of the member, wherein the at least one particle is positioned in an optically interrogatable position with respect to light transmitted through the member to the end portion. The Office Action then alleges that such a particle is taught by Hosokawa.

As an initial matter, without acceding to the correctness of the rejection, independent claim 1 has been amended to recite that the starting portion has a substantially constant average cross- sectional diameter of at least about 100 micrometers and is suitable for guiding the end portion to be

inserted into the cell, the end portion for insertion into the cell has a substantially constant average cross-sectional diameter of less than 100 nm, and at least one particle is attached to the end portion of the member via an adhesive positioned between the at least one particle and the end portion of the member, wherein the adhesive comprises at least one of a polymer or an epoxy. The combination of Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa does not render obvious the combination of features recited in amended independent claim 1.

During the August 26, 2021 interview, independent claim 1 and Rylander were discussed in detail. In particular, Rylander is generally directed to microneedles that are inserted into the skin. The microneedles in Rylander are relatively long, over 2 mm in length, which are necessary due to Rylander's goal of physically penetrating tissue and delivering light directly into a target area below the skin surface. See, e.g., FIG. 1 and the Abstract of Rylander. Such microneedles, due to the fact that they must penetrate through multiple layers of the skin (e.g., the epidermis and the dermis), are required to be both relatively long and relatively thick (e.g., to have sufficient structural integrity when penetrating through the skin). These teachings would accordingly have led one of ordinary skill in the art away from modifying the microneedles in Rylander to have cross-sectional diameters less than 100 nm. See M.P.E.P. § 2143.01(V) (The Proposed Modification Cannot Render the Prior Art Unsatisfactory for Its Intended Purpose).

Furthermore, the needles described in Rylander are either flat microneedles with a non- tapered tip or sharp microneedles with a tapered tip. Both the flat and sharp microneedles have a first taper that becomes increasingly smaller along the length of the needle toward the tip, and the sharp microneedles have a second taper along the tip which is 10-20% of the overall needle length. See, for example, paragraph [0153] and FIG. 7 of Rylander. The needles in Rylander therefore either have a tapered first portion with a flat tip (i.e., flat microneedles), or a tapered first portion and tapered second portion with a sharp tip (i.e., sharp microneedles). None of the needles in Rylander comprise a starting portion having a substantially constant average cross-sectional diameter, an end portion having a substantially constant cross-sectional diameter, and a tapered portion connecting the starting portion to the end portion, as recited in amended independent claim

As discussed during the interview, the Inventors have realized and appreciated that such needles, with relatively long end portions having a substantially constant diameter, cannot be fabricated using conventional technologies. See, for example, pg. 12, lines 5-7 of the application as originally filed. In fact, pg. 7, lines 5-7 of the application as originally filed states that conventional technologies, such as drawing glass rods to produce optical fibers, results in long tapered portions. The needles in Rylander are produced by such methods. See, for example, paragraph [0033] of Rylander, which states, "An exemplary method for manufacturing such fiberoptic needles is by drawing silica fibers into tapered (needle-like) shape by heating the fibers to their melting temperature and stretching them with a mechanical stage." See also paragraphs [0191] and [0195] of Rylander. Thus, articles having the dimensions recited in amended independent claim 1 are neither taught nor suggested by Rylander. Furthermore, nowhere does Rylander teach or suggest techniques that would have allowed one of ordinary skill the art to produce the articles having the claimed shape. Therefore, one of ordinary skill in the art could not have reached the pending claims based on the teachings of Rylander.

In addition to the shape and dimensions of the article, the particle attached to the end portion of the member was also discussed during the August 26, 2021 interview. The particle is important for allowing the article to function as a probe within a cell, e.g., to detect proteins or other intracellular compounds, e.g., using light as discussed in the specification. As recited in amended independent claim 1, the particle is attached to an end portion of the member via an adhesive positioned between the at least one particle and the end portion of the member. The adhesive helps the particle to stay attached to the end portion, without falling off the end portion when the article is inserted into a cell.

It is not seen where Rylander teaches or suggests such a particle. In fact, due to Rylander's goal of penetrating the microneedles through multiple layers of the skin, a particle attached to the microneedles in Rylander would have been expected to be "scraped off' the microneedle. Accordingly, Rylander's teachings would have discouraged one of ordinary skill in the art from using a particle, when the only expected result would be to have the particle be "scraped off." In stark contrast, independent claim 1 as amended herein recites a particle attached to an end portion of the member via an adhesive positioned between the at least one particle and the end portion of the

member, where the adhesive comprises at least one of a polymer or an epoxy. Because Rylander's goal is to insert a microneedle into the skin, Rylander would not reasonably have considered adding an adhesive to the microneedle. Thus, one of ordinary skill in the art would have had no rational reason for modifying Rylander to include an adhesive.

Moreover, the Patent Office alleges that Rylander teaches a member comprising a starting portion having an average cross-sectional diameter of at least about 100 micrometers in Table 4. It is respectfully submitted that the Average Diameter value (i.e., "dAVG") referred to in Table 4 is the average value of the Base Diameter (i.e., "dBAsE") and the Inflection Diameter (i.e., "dINF"), wherein the Base Diameter is the thickness of the microneedle 3 mm from its tip and the Inflection Diameter is the thickness of the microneedle at the junction of the first and second taper. See, for example, paragraphs [0153], [0197], and [0200] and FIG. 7 of Rylander. Therefore, none of the Average Diameter, Base Diameter, or Inflection Diameter values are an accurate representation of the average cross-sectional diameter of a starting portion of the needles in Rylander, since the Base Diameter is a single point measurement on a tapered portion of the needle made a certain distance from the tip (see paragraph [0153] of Rylander), the Inflection Diameter is a single point measurement at the junction of two tapers on the needle, and the Average Diameter is the average of the two values. The Patent Office therefore has not shown that the needles in Rylander comprise a starting portion having an average cross-sectional diameter of at least about 100 micrometers, as recited in independent claim 1.

The Patent Office also alleges that Rylander teaches that the end portion of the needle has a length of between about 750 micrometer and about 3 mm in paragraph [0222]. It is respectfully submitted that the length of 3 mm recited in paragraph [0222] is the overall length of the needle, not the length of just an end portion of the needles in Rylander. The Patent Office therefore has not shown that the needles in Rylander comprise an end portion having a length of between about 750 micrometer and about 3 mm, as recited in independent claim 1.

The Patent Office further alleges that Rylander teaches that the tapered portion has a length of no more than 500 micrometers in FIG. 7 and Table 4. Regarding the "Tip Length (i.e., "LTIp") shown in FIG. 7 and the corresponding values tabulated in Table 4, it is respectfully submitted that the "Tip Length" is the length of the tapered tip of the needles in Rylander. The tip of the needles in

Rylander are the ends of the needles and therefore cannot be considered as the tapered portion, which, as recited in claim 1, connects the starting portion and the end portion. There is nothing that connects to the tip of the needles in Rylander. The Patent Office therefore has not shown that the needles in Rylander comprise a tapered portion having a length of no more than 500 micrometers, as recited in independent claim 1.

Furthermore, it is not seen how Szunerits and Hosokawa cure the deficiencies of Rylander in order to reach the pending claims. For instance, nowhere do either of Szunerits or Hosokawa teach or suggest attaching a particle to a microneedle in such a way as to keep it from becoming "scraped off' while the microneedle is inserted into the skin, as taught in Rylander. Both Szunerits and Hosokawa appear to be directed to detection techniques using metal particles, but neither of these references would have been useful in preventing particles attached to the microneedles from becoming lost as the microneedles were inserted into the skin as taught in Rylander. Thus, one of ordinary skill in the art would have been discouraged from making the proposed combination, as techniques for detecting particles on a microneedle are useless if the particles are no longer there.
For at least the reasons outlined above, the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, and

Hosokawa does not render amended independent claim 1 obvious, and claim 1 is patentable over the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa. The remaining claims that stand rejected on this ground depend from independent claim 1, and are therefore also patentable over the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa for at least the reasons outlined above. Withdrawal of the claim rejections on this ground is respectfully requested.
body.h1: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. # 103 in view of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa and Goncalves
body.p: Claims 142, 143, 145, and 146 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Rylander in view of Szunerits and Hosokawa and further in view of Goncalves, et al., "Self- Assembled Hydrogel Nanoparticles for Drug Delivery Applications," Materials, 2010, 3, 1420- 1460 ("Goncalves").

Claims 142, 143, 145, and 146 depend from independent claim 1, which is patentable over Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa for at least the reasons outlined above. Goncalves fails to cure the deficiencies of Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa noted above with respect to independent

claim 1. Accordingly, claims 142, 143, 145, and 146 are also patentable over the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Goncalves. In addition, it is not conceded that Goncalves teaches any of the features recited in claims 142, 143, 145, and 146, and it is not conceded that it would have been obvious to combine Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Goncalves in the manner suggested in the Office Action. Withdrawal of the claim rejections on this ground is respectfully requested.
body.h1: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. # 103 in view of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Gautam
body.p: Claim 144 stands rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Rylander in view of Szunerits and Hosokawa and further in view of Gautam, et al., "Adsorption kinetics of ammonia sensing by graphene films decorated with platinum nanoparticles," Journal of Applied Physics, 2012, 111, 094317 ("Gautam").

Claim 144 depends from independent claim 1, which is patentable over Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa for at least the reasons outlined above. Gautam fails to cure the deficiencies of Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa noted above with respect to independent claim 1. Accordingly, claim 144 is also patentable over the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Gautam. In addition, it is not conceded that Gautam teaches any of the features recited in claim 144, and it is not conceded that it would have been obvious to combine Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Gautam in the manner suggested in the Office Action. Withdrawal of the claim rejections on this ground is respectfully requested.

In view of the foregoing, this application should now be in condition for allowance. A notice to this effect is respectfully requested. If the Examiner believes, after this response, the application is not in condition for allowance, the Examiner is requested to call the undersigned at the telephone number indicated below to discuss any outstanding issues.

It is believed that no fee is due with this Amendment. However, if a fee is due with this Amendment, please charge our Deposit Account No. 23/2825, under Docket No. H0498.70497US01 from which the undersigned is authorized to draw.
